description: Allegro MicroSystems, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, develops, manufactures, and markets sensor integrated circuits (ICs) and application-specific power ICs for sensing, motion control
trap_reasons: Dividend not covered by free cash flow
description_full: Allegro MicroSystems, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, develops, manufactures, and markets sensor integrated circuits (ICs) and application-specific power ICs for sensing, motion control, and power management functions of complex electromechanical or power conversion systems. Its products include magnetic sensor ICs, such as position, speed, and electric current sensor ICs; and power ICs comprising motor driver ICs, such as regulator, power management ICs, and LED driver ICs, and isolated gate drivers. The company sells its products to original equipment manufacturers and distributors primarily in the automotive and industrial markets through its direct sales force, third party distributors, independent sales representatives, and consignment. The company serves automotive and industrial markets, including advanced industrial markets such as AI data centers, robotics, and energy infrastructure sectors. It operates in the United States, rest of the Americas, Europe, Japan, Greater China, South Korea, and other Asian markets. The company was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Manchester, New Hampshire.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $209K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers, improving at 9%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $29K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $11K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Allegro MicroSystems, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $5.3B market cap on $890M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 11% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 50% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $125M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
Accruals are elevated at -12.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 33% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.09x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-9.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 42% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 37% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 61% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 70% and a beta of 1.41, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.49 vs 5y 1.72), so read it loosely.
About $89.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 46% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $9.42 (margin of safety -199%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 86%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.22 to $14.37 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 176.1 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 31.0 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 42.1 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $48.85 on average, 73% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% earns above the cost of capital of 11.4%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.12).
It runs a 50% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow, or 9% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-12.6% of assets).
It spends 23.1% of revenue on R&D and 5.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($168.8M of cash against $287.3M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.8x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.8, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 143 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.9% over 3 years and 8.5% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (4.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.8% on average.
own: Insiders own 32.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 81%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $960K sold).
Short interest is elevated at 10.6% of the float, 3.7 days to cover.
people: With about 4,250 employees, each generates about $209K of revenue, 0.6x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 8.5% a year.
That works out to $29K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $774K (4x revenue per employee).
